6.3.4 Confidence interval for population mean μ when σ is unknown (small sample)

When σ is known and n is small, then the interval estimator \overline{X}\pm Z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} will still be used for μ but if σ is unknown and n < 30, then the statistic t=\frac{\overline{X}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} is used which has t-distribution with ν = n−1 degrees of freedom and s=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\Sigma(x-\overline{x})^2}. Probability statement can be made as: P\left[-t_{\alpha/2,(\upsilon)}<t<t_{\alpha/2,(\upsilon)}\right]=1-\alpha

Putting value of t to have a 100(1−α)% confidence interval for μ when σ is unknown and n is small as;

$\overline{X}\pm t_{\alpha/2,(\upsilon)}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$

■ Degrees of freedom

The number of values in the sample that are independent and free to vary is called degrees of freedom e.g. if x_1+x_2=10. we can give value only to x_1 or x_2 the second one will be automatically computed. Hence d.f = 2 − 1 = 1. Generally if we have x_1+x_2+\ldots\ldots x_n=10 we can gave values to first n−1 scores freely and one score is restricted, so we have degrees freedom d.f = n−1
